title: CSS Formatter: The Limits of Formatting, Minifying, and Sorting
description: How the CSS formatter works: token rules, what minifying removes, why property sorting is alphabetical, and how sorting can change the cascade.
content:
The CSS formatter splits a chunk of CSS into tokens on {, }, and ;, then reflows them into indented lines. The same page can also minify the code onto a single line and sort properties alphabetically. It uses string splitting rather than a CSS parser, so it does no syntax validation—and once property sorting is enabled, the output can even change the final styles.

Three actions, one splitting rule

There are only three transformations: format, minify, and format with property sorting enabled. All three share the same tokenize(): it scans the input character by character, and only a {, }, or ; at bracket depth 0 cuts the accumulated text into a token; those three symbols also each become a token of their own. Depth increases on ( or [ and decreases on ) or ] (never below 0), so the semicolons and braces inside url(...) and rgba(...) are not treated as separators.

This rule also marks the ceiling on what the tool can do: it recognizes symbol positions, not CSS syntax, and does not judge whether selectors or property names are valid. Minifying takes the same tokenizing path; only the way the tokens are joined back together differs.

Formatting: add semicolons, split declarations at the first colon

Formatting generates lines one by one from the token sequence. On {, the selector or at-rule prelude accumulated so far is written on a new line with { appended, and depth increases by one; on }, a declaration still missing its semicolon first gets one, then } gets a line of its own and depth decreases by one; on ;, the current declaration is closed off as a line. Indentation comes in only two settings, 2 spaces and 4 spaces.

Inside a block (depth greater than 0), a token containing a colon whose next token is not { is split at the first colon into “property: value,” and any remaining colons in the value are joined back as they were—so a value such as background: url(https://…) is not broken apart. There are four rules:

  • Comments are discarded wholesale during tokenizing, and no space is inserted in their place: characters touching either side of a comment get glued together, so a/**/b becomes ab; an unclosed /* swallows everything to the end of the input.
  • Strings inside quotes are not split, and a backslash skips the next character, so an escaped quote does not end the string early.
  • A ; or { } inside brackets takes no part in splitting, so semicolons in data URIs and commas in functions are safe.
  • Selector and at-rule preludes only have leading and trailing whitespace trimmed; internal newlines and spaces are kept as they are, so a selector list written across several lines still carries newlines after formatting; the indentation prefix is added at the start of the line according to the current nesting depth, so at top level (depth 0) neither line is indented, and only the first line inside a nested block carries the prefix.

Formatting therefore only translates symbol positions into line breaks and indentation; it does not rearrange the code into a canonical form: it does not regroup selectors, merge duplicate declarations, or add units to values, and the only character it ever adds is that semicolon at the end of a block.

Minifying: only whitespace, trailing semicolons, and the space after a colon

Minifying concatenates the tokens directly, then runs a round of regex replacements: it removes a semicolon immediately before }, strips whitespace around the four symbols { } ; ,, compresses “: ” to “:,” and collapses any other run of whitespace to a single space. Quoted strings are protected separately and their contents are left untouched; multi-line values inside brackets are collapsed to at most one space.

Values themselves are out of scope: there is no color shortening (#ffffff does not become #fff), no unit removal for zero values (0px does not become 0), and no spaces added to calc(). Per the specification, the + and - inside calc() must have whitespace on both sides; the tool only preserves what you wrote and will not add it for you, so calc(100%-1em) is still invalid after minifying. An existing single space survives, while extra whitespace is collapsed to one.

Empty input is handled inconsistently on the two sides: formatting first checks whether the input is empty and shows “Please enter CSS” when it is; minifying has no such check, so empty input still reports “Minification complete” while the output box stays empty.

Property sorting: alphabetical, and only adjacent declarations

With “Property sorting” enabled, the tool makes another pass over the lines it has already generated. Whether a line counts as a declaration is decided by two hard conditions: after indentation is removed it starts with a property name (word characters or hyphens) followed by a colon, and the whole line ends with a semicolon. Only such lines enter the list to be sorted; the sort key is the property name, compared as a locale-aware string comparison (localeCompare) rather than by cascade priority.

On a non-declaration line—a selector line, {, }, an @media prelude, a blank line—the current pending list is sorted and stitched back before the scan continues. The sorting scope is therefore limited to adjacent declarations inside the same block: declarations separated by }, an @media rule, or a nested rule keep their relative positions. The sort is stable, so when the same property is written twice (for example two display declarations used as a fallback), their order is preserved.

Two knock-on effects: comments are already gone by the tokenizing stage, so a comment that used to sit between two declarations is not in the line array, and those two declarations become adjacent and are sorted together; custom properties (such as --brand-color) and prefixed properties meet the same test and are sorted as well.

Why sorting can change the final styles

When the browser decides which declaration in the same rule block wins, it looks at source order: at equal specificity, the later declaration overrides the earlier one. A shorthand property also resets all the longhand properties it covers—font resets font-size, font-weight, and line-height; background resets background-color and background-image; border resets border-color and border-width. Put the two rules together and sorting acquires a side effect.

Suppose the same block writes font-size first and font second. Without sorting, font comes last, resets the font size, and overrides the earlier font-size. Alphabetically, font is a prefix of font-size and the shorter string sorts first, so after sorting font moves up and font-size lands last; the font size is now decided by font-size, and the size written inside font no longer applies. At no point does the tool do anything but compare property-name strings—nothing in the process understands this relationship.

The same holds for three common combinations:

ShorthandLonghands it resetsWithout sortingWith sorting enabled
fontfont-sizefont is written later, so the size comes from the shorthandfont moves up, font-size is written later and takes effect
backgroundbackground-colorbackground is written later, so the color comes from the shorthandbackground moves up, background-color is written later and takes effect
borderborder-color, border-widthborder is written later, so color and width come from the shorthandborder moves up, and the matching longhands are written later and take effect

The reverse is equally true: a block that originally writes font first and font-size second keeps the same order after sorting, and the result does not change. Sorting does not make anything more correct; it just reorders “who is written later” alphabetically. Nor is it a cascade-priority tool: it ignores specificity and !important, and it does not move declarations between blocks. If you want to sort, expand shorthands into longhands first, or avoid mixing these pairs inside one block; after sorting, check the computed styles in the developer tools, which is more reliable than reading the output text.

Which action when: three paths

  1. Reading code someone else minified: paste it, choose 2 spaces, click Format, and understand the structure before editing—leave sorting off.
  2. Minifying before delivery: confirm the source already renders correctly in the browser, then click Minify and copy the result; strings and data URIs stay intact, but comments and the semicolon at the end of a block disappear.
  3. Standardizing property order: enable sorting only on rules whose entire block uses longhands; expand blocks containing shorthands by hand first, then process them in batches.

The tool only handles CSS text. To tidy up HTML structure, use the HTML Formatter; to work on JavaScript, use the JS Formatter; and to match some selector text inside a stylesheet, use the Regex Tester.

Boundaries and limitations

  • No syntax validation: formatting only checks whether the input is empty, and any non-empty input is laid out and reported as “Formatting complete”; minifying does not even have that check. There is no CSS parser, no error line numbers, and no warnings, so invalid CSS gets the same “complete” message.
  • No syntax fixes: it does not balance missing brackets, add units or prefixes, merge duplicate rules, or deduplicate declarations, and it does not recognize SCSS/Less // comments or $variable—those are simply moved around as ordinary text.
  • Sorting ignores the cascade: the only basis is the alphabetical order of property names; it neither understands that shorthands reset longhands nor considers !important and specificity, and it never moves declarations across rule blocks.
  • External resources are untouched: @import is just a line of text; the file it points to is never loaded or inlined.
  • Whitespace-sensitive spots need a human look: minifying removes whitespace around symbols and after colons, and extra whitespace inside calc() is reduced to one space; strings are preserved verbatim, and all other layout becomes tighter.
  • Synchronous on the main thread: a click runs tokenizing and regex work to completion in one go, with no progress and no cancel; a large file keeps occupying the page, and an unclosed string or comment can make the splitting diverge from what you expect.

One more point: the page is static HTML plus in-browser scripts, input is never sent to a server, and refreshing loses it. Because it does no validation, do not treat “Formatting complete” as proof that the code is usable—check in the browser whether the styles take effect.

faqs.q: Can property sorting change how my styles look?
faqs.a: Yes, if the same block mixes a shorthand with its corresponding longhands. Sorting only follows the alphabetical order of property names, so font sorts before font-size, and the font-size written later ends up winning instead. A block that uses only longhands is generally unaffected. If you want to sort, expand the shorthands into longhands first, then check the computed styles in the developer tools after sorting.

faqs.q: Does the “Formatting complete” message mean the code is fine?
faqs.a: No. The tool only checks whether the input is empty, then runs tokenizing and layout directly; there is no CSS parser, and no error line numbers or warnings. Minifying does not even have the empty-input check, so empty content still reports “Minification complete.”

faqs.q: Does minifying change strings or data URIs?
faqs.a: No. Content inside quotes is kept in full, and semicolons inside brackets take no part in splitting, so values such as url(data:...;base64,...) pass through unchanged; what gets removed is comments, the semicolon at the end of a block, and whitespace around symbols. The values themselves are not shortened or stripped of units.

faqs.q: Why do all the comments disappear after formatting?
faqs.a: During tokenizing, a /* */ comment is discarded wholesale and no space is inserted in its place, so characters touching either side of the comment stick together and a/**/b becomes ab; an unclosed /* swallows everything to the end of the input. If you want to keep an explanation, do not put it in this CSS.

focus: Tokens are split by bracket depth and then reflowed: formatting only adds the semicolon at the end of a block, minifying only squeezes whitespace and symbols, and property sorting only follows the alphabetical order of property names, so it can reverse which of a shorthand and a longhand wins.
notice: The tool runs locally in your browser, so your CSS is never uploaded. It does no syntax validation, and “Formatting complete” does not mean the code is valid.
